notes: Five-minute pass: README, landing, demo report, connect (qa/reports/ui). Strong: a transferable decision lesson. You get the break-even (9 a day against a guess of 8), the worst case as a share of spare cash (€560, 37%), the guess that matters most (€756 swing), a keep/tweak/stop test card and 'Use this method again' (report.txt:804-894). I redid the sums; they hold. It is honest and demo data is labelled everywhere. Original: MCP plus a report that lives in its link, and an imagined-customer rehearsal that yields questions, not forecasts. Held back: (1) In the demo the AI does nothing visible. Code does the maths and the rehearsal says 'Played by simple fixed rules, with no AI' (report.txt:524), while the caveat above says 'played by an AI' (report.txt:516, src/sim/rehearsal.ts:53), on the very distinction it teaches. (2) 'What you learned' (report.txt:868-873) has no lesson about AI. (3) The feedback loop (landing step 7) is never shown. (4) There is no live URL (README.md:26-29: YOUR-SITE). (5) No evidence that a real owner has used it.
improvements: Demo report, step 1 and step 5 (src/report/demo.ts:3, src/report/sections.ts, src/report/rehearsal.ts): make the AI's work visible. Add a collapsible 'How this report was made' panel to step 1. It shows the 5-6 questions the AI asked, each with its 'why it matters', and says which tool calculated what ('the AI asked and explained; code did the sums'). Then replace the rule-based demo rehearsal with a saved AI-played run, labelled 'played by Claude on <date>, saved for this demo'. Why: 'use of AI' is a judging criterion, and today the demo shows only deterministic code and fixed rules. Done when a judge on the demo can point to one thing the AI did and one thing code did within 60 seconds.

Report, 'What you learned' (report.txt:868-873) and the glossary (report.txt:896-906): add an explicit lesson about AI, in the owner's numbers. For example: '24 figures here were worked out by plain arithmetic, not by the AI'; '4 numbers are guesses: no AI can know them, only your test can'; 'the 6 customers were imagined: 0 of 6 trying it says nothing about your street'. Add a transferable rule: 'Next time any AI gives you a number, ask: is it mine, calculated, a guess or imagined?' Add the glossary entry 'AI model: explains and role-plays; it does not know your future'. Why: the track is AI education, and the current takeaways are all about the decision. Done when the Selin and educator persona files can each state an AI lesson in their own words.

src/sim/rehearsal.ts:53 and src/report/rehearsal.ts:20/230: fix the contradiction in the demo. The caveat says 'played by an AI' and the mode line says 'with no AI' (report.txt:516 and 524). Make the caveat follow the rehearsal mode. Also remove the 'Your number' chip from 'Check these with real customers': that card holds questions, not owner data. Why: honesty is the core of the AI lesson, and a wrong label on the very thing the labels teach undermines it. Done when report.txt makes exactly one claim about who played the customers, and source chips appear only beside numbers.

Landing step 7 'Learn' (site/index.html) and a second demo link: show the feedback loop. Publish a clearly labelled demo 'after the test' report (built from whatif_log_result output) that puts the counted extra customers next to cautious, expected and optimistic, and says which guess was closest and what changes next time. Why: predicting and then checking is the strongest teaching moment and the clearest difference from a chatbot, and today it is only described. Done when landing step 7 links to a report that shows 'what happened' beside the three scenarios.

README.md:1-29 and the demo ribbon (src/report/sections.ts:56): make it possible to try in 60 seconds. Deploy, then put the live demo-report link and the real MCP URL in the first lines of the README. Turn 'Swap in your own to get your answer' into a link to /connect with a copyable first prompt. Why: README step 1 says 'Open the site', but no site is named, so a judge cannot try it. Execution and demo are scored. Done when the README's first screen has a working URL and the ribbon has a next step.

README or the landing page: add honest proof of use. vision.md:39 says one session with a real café owner is stronger proof than features. Run one session, then report what the owner understood, the break-even they found, and whether they would run the test, in their words and with their permission. Never invent a quote. Why: 'would you believe a real owner tried it?' is currently unanswered. Done when there is a dated note of one real session, even a short one.
pitchIn60s: What-IF is an MCP connector plus a skill. It turns 'what if I run a weekday lunch deal?' into a six-step visual lesson. Every one of the owner's numbers is labelled as theirs, a guess, calculated or imagined. Code works out the break-even and the worst case, and a slider shows why the result moves. An imagined-customer rehearsal yields questions, not forecasts, and the report ends with a printable 10-day test with a stop rule. It teaches the method, not just the answer, and it is honest and polished. The gaps: in the demo the AI's own contribution is invisible (even self-contradicting), there is no live link to try, and there is no evidence yet that a real owner has used it.
standout: The test card: a baseline count, a tally sheet, a €370 cost cap and a keep/tweak/stop rule agreed before the results. A café could actually run it on Monday, and it turns a guess into evidence.
weakest: Use of AI. The demo shows deterministic maths and a rule-based rehearsal, the caveat says both 'played by an AI' and 'with no AI', and no take-home lesson about AI is stated.
